item.title: Fatty Acid Saturation and the Physical State of Fats
item.stimulus:
A food science class extracted fats (triglycerides) from three sources. Each fat molecule contains three fatty acid tails. The students used a lab analysis service to find the percentage of fatty acid tails in each sample that fall into three categories. The results are shown below. Each row totals 100 percent.

Sample | Saturated tails (%) | Tails with one C=C double bond (%) | Tails with two or more C=C double bonds (%)
X | 52 | 42 | 6
Y | 14 | 73 | 13
Z | 10 | 20 | 70

All three samples were kept at room temperature (20 °C) before testing.
item.model_answer:
(a) A saturated fatty acid tail has only single bonds between its carbon atoms, so the chain is straight. An unsaturated tail has at least one carbon-to-carbon double bond, and each double bond puts a kink (bend) in the carbon chain.

(b) Sample X is most likely solid at room temperature. It has 52% saturated tails, compared with 14% for Y and 10% for Z, so only 48% of its tails are unsaturated, the least of the three samples. Saturated tails are straight and can pack closely together, while the kinks caused by double bonds keep unsaturated tails from packing tightly. The more unsaturated a fat is, the more liquid it is at room temperature, so the least unsaturated fat, X, is the one most likely to be solid.

(c) The fatty acid tails of the fat are long hydrocarbon chains that are nonpolar, so the fat is hydrophobic. Water is polar, and its molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another. The nonpolar fat cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, so the water molecules stay attracted to each other and exclude the fat, which collects as a separate layer.

(d) First, the fat is an energy store: the seal can break it down for energy when food is scarce. Second, the layer of fat under the skin insulates the body, reducing heat loss so the seal stays warm in cold water.
item.verification_python:
rows = {'X': (52, 42, 6), 'Y': (14, 73, 13), 'Z': (10, 20, 70)}
for k, v in rows.items():
    assert sum(v) == 100
unsat = {k: 100 - v[0] for k, v in rows.items()}
assert unsat['X'] == 48
assert unsat['Y'] == 86
assert unsat['Z'] == 90
most_sat = max(rows, key=lambda k: rows[k][0])
assert most_sat == 'X'
assert min(unsat, key=unsat.get) == 'X'
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

item.title: Fatty Acid Double Bonds and Melting Points
item.stimulus:
Students compare four fatty acids. Each has an 18-carbon chain, but they differ in the number of carbon-carbon double bonds in the chain. The students look up the approximate melting point of each fatty acid. Room temperature in the laboratory is 25°C.

Fatty acid | Carbon atoms | C=C double bonds | Approximate melting point (°C)
Stearic acid | 18 | 0 | 69
Oleic acid | 18 | 1 | 13
Linoleic acid | 18 | 2 | −5
Linolenic acid | 18 | 3 | −11
item.model_answer:
(a) Stearic acid is the saturated fatty acid. Its carbon chain has only single bonds between carbon atoms, with 0 C=C double bonds.

(b) As the number of double bonds increases, the melting point decreases. With 0 double bonds, stearic acid melts at 69°C. Oleic acid (1 double bond) melts at 13°C, linoleic acid (2) at −5°C, and linolenic acid (3) at −11°C.

(c) Oleic acid has one double bond, which puts a kink in its carbon chain. The kinked chains cannot pack closely together, so less heat is needed to separate them, and the melting point is only 13°C. Room temperature (25°C) is above that, so oleic acid is a liquid. Stearic acid has only single bonds, so its chains are straight and pack tightly. Its melting point of 69°C is well above 25°C, so it is a solid.

(d) I predict the fish's stored fat is made mostly of fatty acids with two or more double bonds. At 4°C, stearic acid (melting point 69°C) and oleic acid (13°C) would both be solid. Only linoleic acid (−5°C) and linolenic acid (−11°C) have melting points below 4°C and would stay liquid. Since the fat remains liquid at 4°C, it must be rich in these more unsaturated fatty acids.
item.verification_python:
data = {'stearic': (0, 69), 'oleic': (1, 13), 'linoleic': (2, -5), 'linolenic': (3, -11)}
ordered = sorted(data.values())
mps = [mp for db, mp in ordered]
assert all(mps[i] > mps[i+1] for i in range(len(mps)-1))
sat = [k for k, v in data.items() if v[0] == 0]
assert sat == ['stearic']
room = 25
assert data['stearic'][1] > room
assert data['oleic'][1] < room
fish = 4
liquid_at_4 = sorted(k for k, v in data.items() if v[1] < fish)
assert liquid_at_4 == ['linoleic', 'linolenic']
assert all(data[k][0] >= 2 for k in liquid_at_4)
assert data['oleic'][1] > fish and data['stearic'][1] > fish
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

item.title: Fatty Acid Double Bonds and Melting Point
item.stimulus:
A student compares four fatty acids. Each has an 18-carbon chain, but they differ in the number of carbon-carbon double bonds in the chain. The student looks up the melting point of each fatty acid. A substance is liquid at a given temperature if that temperature is above its melting point.

Fatty acid | Carbon atoms | C=C double bonds | Melting point (°C)
Stearic acid | 18 | 0 | 69.3
Oleic acid | 18 | 1 | 13.4
Linoleic acid | 18 | 2 | −5
Alpha-linolenic acid | 18 | 3 | −11

The student then studies a fish species that lives in water at 4 °C. The fish's body temperature matches the water temperature, and its stored fat remains liquid at this body temperature.
item.model_answer:
(a) As the number of carbon-carbon double bonds increases, the melting point decreases. Stearic acid, with 0 double bonds, melts at 69.3 °C, oleic acid (1) at 13.4 °C, linoleic acid (2) at −5 °C, and alpha-linolenic acid (3) at −11 °C.

(b) Stearic acid is saturated, with only single bonds between carbons, so its chain is straight. Each double bond in an unsaturated fatty acid causes a kink in the carbon chain. The kinked chains cannot pack tightly against one another, so attractions between neighboring molecules are weaker and fewer. Less energy is needed to separate them, so the unsaturated fatty acid melts at a lower temperature.

(c) Oleic acid, linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid are liquid at 22 °C, because 22 °C is above their melting points. Stearic acid (melting point 69.3 °C) is solid.

(d) The fish's fat should be made mainly of fatty acids with two or more double bonds. At 4 °C, stearic acid (69.3 °C) and oleic acid (13.4 °C) would be solid because 4 °C is below their melting points. Linoleic acid (−5 °C) and alpha-linolenic acid (−11 °C) melt below 4 °C, so only these more unsaturated fatty acids would keep the stored fat liquid at the fish's body temperature.
item.verification_python:
data = {'stearic': (0, 69.3), 'oleic': (1, 13.4), 'linoleic': (2, -5.0), 'linolenic': (3, -11.0)}
items = sorted(data.values())
for i in range(len(items) - 1):
    assert items[i][1] > items[i + 1][1]
liquid_room = sorted(k for k, v in data.items() if 22 > v[1])
assert liquid_room == sorted(['oleic', 'linoleic', 'linolenic'])
liquid_fish = sorted(k for k, v in data.items() if 4 > v[1])
assert liquid_fish == sorted(['linoleic', 'linolenic'])
assert all(data[k][0] >= 2 for k in liquid_fish)
assert all(data[k][0] < 2 for k in data if k not in liquid_fish)
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

item.title: Fatty Acid Saturation and Melting Point of Fats
item.stimulus:
Students extracted triglycerides (fats) from four sources. For each sample they determined three things: the percentage of fatty acid tails that are saturated, the mean number of carbon–carbon double bonds per fatty acid tail, and the melting point. They also recorded the physical state of each sample at room temperature (20 °C). Results are shown below.

Sample | Saturated tails (%) | Mean C=C double bonds per tail | Melting point (°C) | State at 20 °C
W (beef fat) | 52 | 0.45 | 42 | solid
X (pork fat) | 40 | 0.65 | 30 | solid
Y (olive oil) | 14 | 1.0 | −6 | liquid
Z (safflower oil) | 9 | 1.6 | −20 | liquid
item.model_answer:
(a) A saturated fatty acid tail has only single bonds between its carbon atoms. An unsaturated fatty acid tail has at least one carbon–carbon double bond.

(b) As the mean number of double bonds per tail increases, the melting point decreases. Sample W has 0.45 double bonds per tail and melts at 42 °C. Sample Z has 1.6 double bonds per tail and melts at −20 °C. X (0.65, 30 °C) and Y (1.0, −6 °C) fall in between and follow the same pattern.

(c) Most of Z's tails are unsaturated. The double bonds in these tails cause kinks in the carbon chains. Kinked tails cannot pack tightly against one another, so the attractions between neighboring molecules are weaker. Less heat is needed to separate the molecules, which gives Z a melting point (−20 °C) far below 20 °C, so Z is liquid. W has many straight, saturated tails that pack closely together. The stronger attractions between these tails give W a melting point of 42 °C, so W is solid at 20 °C.

(d) Sample V will be liquid at 20 °C. V has 1.2 double bonds per tail, which is more than sample Y (1.0). Y is already liquid at 20 °C with a melting point of −6 °C. Because more double bonds lower the melting point, V's melting point should be below −6 °C, likely between −6 °C and −20 °C, which is well below 20 °C.
item.verification_python:
samples = {'W': (52, 0.45, 42, 'solid'), 'X': (40, 0.65, 30, 'solid'), 'Y': (14, 1.0, -6, 'liquid'), 'Z': (9, 1.6, -20, 'liquid')}
room = 20
for k, (sat, db, mp, state) in samples.items():
    assert (mp > room) == (state == 'solid')
order = sorted(samples, key=lambda k: samples[k][1])
mps = [samples[k][2] for k in order]
assert all(mps[i] > mps[i+1] for i in range(len(mps)-1))
sats = [samples[k][0] for k in order]
assert all(sats[i] > sats[i+1] for i in range(len(sats)-1))
v_db = 1.2

item.title: Fatty Acid Double Bonds and Melting Point
item.stimulus:
A student investigates how the structure of fatty acids affects their physical properties. The student compares four fatty acids. Each has a chain of 18 carbon atoms but differs in the number of carbon-carbon double bonds in its hydrocarbon tail. The student records the melting point of each fatty acid from a reference source and notes its state at room temperature (20°C).

Fatty acid | Number of C=C double bonds | Melting point (°C) | State at 20°C
Stearic acid | 0 | 69 | Solid
Oleic acid | 1 | 13 | Liquid
Linoleic acid | 2 | -5 | Liquid
Linolenic acid | 3 | -11 | Liquid
item.model_answer:
(a) Stearic acid has only single bonds between its carbon atoms, so it is a saturated fatty acid. Oleic acid has one carbon-carbon double bond in its tail, so it is unsaturated. Stearic acid is the saturated one.

(b) As the number of carbon-carbon double bonds increases, the melting point decreases. Stearic acid, with 0 double bonds, melts at 69°C, while linolenic acid, with 3 double bonds, melts at -11°C.

(c) Each double bond causes a kink (bend) in the hydrocarbon chain. The kinked tails cannot pack closely together the way straight saturated tails can, so the molecules are held together less tightly. Less energy is needed to separate them, so the melting point is lower and the lipid is more liquid at room temperature. More double bonds means more kinks and an even lower melting point.

(d) The fat will be liquid at 20°C. Each of its three linolenic acid tails has three double bonds, so the fat is highly unsaturated and its tails are heavily kinked and cannot pack tightly. The more unsaturated a lipid is, the more liquid it is at room temperature; linolenic acid itself melts at -11°C, far below 20°C.

    assert data[i][1] > data[i+1][1]
assert data[0][1] > room
for db, mp in data[1:]:
    assert mp < room
assert data[-1][1] == -11 and data[0][1] == 69

item.title: Fatty Acid Double Bonds and Melting Point
item.stimulus:
A student studies how the structure of fatty acids affects their physical properties. The student obtains four fatty acids, each with a carbon chain 18 carbons long, and records the number of carbon-carbon double bonds in each chain along with each fatty acid's approximate melting point. Room temperature in the lab is about 22 °C.

Fatty acid | Number of C=C double bonds | Approximate melting point (°C)
Stearic acid | 0 | 69
Oleic acid | 1 | 13
Linoleic acid | 2 | -5
Linolenic acid | 3 | -11
item.model_answer:
(a) Stearic acid contains only single bonds between its carbon atoms, so it is a saturated fatty acid. Oleic acid contains one carbon-carbon double bond, so it is an unsaturated fatty acid.

(b) As the number of carbon-carbon double bonds increases, the melting point decreases. Stearic acid (0 double bonds) melts at about 69 °C, while linolenic acid (3 double bonds) melts at about -11 °C.

(c) Each double bond causes a kink in the carbon chain. Kinked chains cannot pack tightly against neighboring chains, so the molecules are held together less closely and less energy is needed to separate them. This lowers the melting point, so the more unsaturated a fatty acid is, the more liquid it is at a given temperature.

(d) The oil is mostly linoleic acid. Linoleic acid has a melting point of about -5 °C, which is below 4 °C, so it remains liquid in the refrigerator. Stearic acid melts at about 69 °C, far above 4 °C, so an oil made mostly of stearic acid would be solid at 4 °C (and even at room temperature, 22 °C).
